Checklist item: Define the program goals at the start
Brief example: Recruit students, introduce career paths, or bring STEM to high-need areas

Checklist item: Decide how you will measure success
Brief example: Headcounts, surveys, quotes, or tracking where students go next
Source: Computing center staff, High school educator, Outreach coordinator

Checklist item: Draft a budget by category before committing to an activity type
Brief example: Categories used by one computing center: off-campus and on-campus activities, food, equipment, consumables such as T-shirts, housing for staff and students, wifi
Variant note: Cost categories may be smaller for a presentation vs workshops or camps. Housing applies only to on-campus camps

Checklist item: Start by finding ways to run the activity with the money and resources you already have
Brief example: Piggyback on programs already on campus, then collect data and refine

Checklist item: List potential funding sources and check each one
Brief example: Federal grants with broader-impacts requirements, industry partners, local family foundations, alumni gifts, units that already fund outreach
Source: Computing center staff, Outreach program staff, Outreach coordinator, Faculty member

Checklist item: Ask faculty about adding your activity to their grant's broader impacts
Brief example: Faculty look for ways to strengthen broader impacts, even a 1 to 2 hour collaboration

Checklist item: Check with the development office and sponsored projects office before approaching donors or funders
Brief example: Development offices may want to manage relationships with foundations and donors
Variant note: Know your own org chart

Checklist item: Check industry partners' giving or community pages to see what they already support
Brief example: Look at a company's community or giving page for available grants

Checklist item: Decide whether to charge a fee, and plan scholarships if you do
Brief example: One university camp charges $150 per camp with needs-based scholarships; another camp's fee was $750 per week, raised to $900, with about half of students on scholarship
Variant note: Overnight camps cost more than day camps

Checklist item: Consider a cost-recovery fee for items such as lunch and operating costs
Brief example: Example: a full-day workshop with lunch may carry a fee to cover lunch and operational costs

Checklist item: Decide how staff, teachers, and student workers will be paid, if at all
Brief example: Pay chaperones a stipend. Pay staff for meeting and camp hours. Consider if faculty and staff could count the activity as part of their job.

Checklist item: Consider funding or compensating K-12 teachers who contribute
Brief example: A district contact said a university is more successful if it can fund or compensate teachers for their work

Checklist item: Plan how to sustain the activity if grant funding ends
Brief example: Tuition-based camps can fund a free event; one computing center suggests finding creative ways to sustain programs

Checklist item: Outline a way to track costs for later reporting
Brief example: Tracked costs can help show funders what the activity needs

Checklist item: Name one lead organizer and one point of contact
Brief example: A single contact for youth protection matters, and a single person for parent communication

Checklist item: Define roles: instructors, helpers, chaperones, logistics support
Brief example: One computing center co-teaches with a supervisor and brings in staff and grad students as guest teachers
Variant note: Presentations need fewer roles than workshops or camps

Checklist item: Ask which staff and volunteers are interested before assigning outreach work
Brief example: One director said outreach depends on which staff want to do it, and it is hard to sustain if they leave

Checklist item: Recruit grad students, undergraduates, and other campus staff as helpers or guest speakers
Brief example: Grad students may relate well to high schoolers; undergraduates can be camp mentors

Checklist item: Plan supervision ratios and ask your youth protection office what they require
Brief example: One university's day camps: 1 trained person per 18 youth; overnight camps are stricter. One computing center notes a preferred ratio of 2:1 or 3:1 and says to check state requirements
Variant note: Ratios differ by age, overnight status, and campus
Source: University compliance staff, Computing center staff

Checklist item: Plan for at least two trained staff at all times
Brief example: One university's youth protection office recommends two trained people on staff at all times, and two when taking youth off campus

Checklist item: Invite local K-12 teachers to help
Brief example: Teachers can recruit students, chaperone, and help students feel comfortable; usually 2 high school teachers helped at one university's camps

Checklist item: Plan for counselor or chaperone hiring and training time
Brief example: Hiring counselors alone can take about a month and a half
Variant note: Chaperones who stay in the dorm are on-campus camp only

Checklist item: Consider a dedicated events person or professional to handle logistics
Brief example: One director advised not to try to do it all yourself

Checklist item: Have a plan B for staffing surprises
Brief example: Example: a partner's chaperones changed their role in year 2 or 3

Checklist item: Check staff workload and wellbeing before committing
Brief example: High school camps are a lot for staff to take on

Checklist item: Choose hands-on, interactive activities over lecture
Brief example: Take apart old servers, Raspberry Pi projects, VR activities, robot dogs
Source: Computing center staff, Outreach coordinator, High school educator

Checklist item: Set a learning goal for each activity, then fit the topic to it
Brief example: If the goal is to learn to be a scientist, build a project step by step; if it is career exposure, plan a field trip

Checklist item: Build the curriculum around a faculty or staff member who is excited about the topic
Brief example: Find the person first, then build the curriculum around them

Checklist item: Adapt existing lectures and materials for high schoolers
Brief example: Use what faculty already have, but tweak it for the age group and keep it less intense
Source: Faculty member, Computing center staff, Outreach coordinator

Checklist item: If no faculty member is teaching, ask one to suggest, teach, or check your materials
Brief example: Or build an HPC demo with some relevance to a field

Checklist item: Check the age and skill range of participants
Brief example: Math levels vary widely by grade; some programs recruit rising juniors and seniors

Checklist item: Build in breaks and avoid overfilling the schedule
Brief example: One university cut back activities and tours after year 1; one tour may be enough

Checklist item: Plan how students will get computer access
Brief example: Loaner laptops, computer labs, or asking students to bring laptops

Checklist item: Use group projects if students will be on internet-connected computers
Brief example: Students may get distracted by games or news

Checklist item: Connect what students learn to careers
Brief example: Field trips, career talks, and showing a pathway beyond a four-year degree
Source: Faculty member, Computing center staff, High school educator

Checklist item: Plan a showcase at the end of the program
Brief example: Poster session, group project presentation, or short whiteboard videos

Checklist item: Plan relaxed evening activities for overnight programs
Brief example: Snacks, board games, or a movie; no homework
Variant note: On-campus camp only

Checklist item: Let students take something home when possible
Brief example: Give students tools they can show family; check item cost first
Variant note: Raspberry Pi prices rose, so check before promising

Checklist item: Ask whether a similar program already exists on campus before starting from scratch
Brief example: Two computing centers partnered with their university's pre-college and summer programs, which handled admissions, housing, and meals
Variant note: Start small: partner with an existing program and provide the content

Checklist item: Talk to other people running K-12 programs on your campus
Brief example: One director talked to anyone they knew doing K-12 work on campus
Source: Computing center staff, Outreach program staff

Checklist item: Find domain experts on campus
Brief example: Faculty, grad students, and campus units with relevant equipment or spaces
Source: Faculty member, Computing center staff, Outreach coordinator

Checklist item: Identify a district or school contact
Brief example: One district contact suggested identifying the main contact in the district as step one

Checklist item: Reach out to local K-12 teachers
Brief example: Teachers know students well and can promote the program; once they know what you offer, they keep coming back

Checklist item: Offer teachers something in return
Brief example: Professional development, a stipend, or a role in the program
Source: Computing center staff, School district staff

Checklist item: Find local companies and alumni
Brief example: Tours, career talks, volunteers, and funding
Source: Faculty member, High school educator, Outreach coordinator

Checklist item: Explore state or national programs you can join
Brief example: Examples from interviews include a national robotics program and a university-wide summer camp program
Source: Outreach program staff, Outreach coordinator, Computing center staff

Checklist item: Connect with organizations that serve specific student groups
Brief example: MS-CC, Upward Bound, and Women in HPC chapters
Source: Computing center staff, Pre-college program director

Checklist item: Choose partners with aligned goals
Brief example: Piggybacking on another program can work, but its goals may differ from yours

Checklist item: Choose a pitch that matches your audience
Brief example: Pipeline for enrollment for leadership; outreach mission for higher leadership; career pipeline for the field

Checklist item: Check whether outreach fits your unit's mission or strategic plan
Brief example: Some units have no outreach in their strategic plan; one computing center wrote a strategic plan with a vision before expanding

Checklist item: Identify who needs to approve or be informed
Brief example: Dean, director, or the vice president for research, depending on your org chart
Source: Computing center staff, Outreach program staff

Checklist item: Plan for common concerns: money and staff time
Brief example: One director said resistance is usually about money and time

Checklist item: Collect data from early events to use in later requests
Brief example: Buy-in got easier once a program had run and had data

Checklist item: Find the existing campus offices that already support youth programs
Brief example: If you see summer programs on campus, some office is supporting them; ask those organizers who helped them
Variant note: Tips for finding offices

Checklist item: Ask each office what to ask, what to watch for, and how far ahead to start
Brief example: Forms, deadlines, fees, and approvals

Checklist item: Build a timeline that works backward from the event date
Brief example: One organizer copies a day-by-day spreadsheet each year, with a calendar for advertising, ordering supplies, and hiring

Checklist item: Reserve rooms and know how students will get into buildings
Brief example: Locked doors, breakout rooms, and equipment limits

Checklist item: Arrange computers, equipment, and internet
Brief example: Work with IT for labs or loaners

Checklist item: Choose hours that work for families
Brief example: Camp hours that do not fit working families can keep students out

Checklist item: Choose a date that avoids conflicts
Brief example: One school held its event between athletic seasons and alongside parent-teacher night

Checklist item: Housing: contact the residence hall or housing office early
Brief example: One computing center asks its campus housing office in Sept or Oct for summer rooms; another university's housing office starts collecting requests in Oct
Variant note: On-campus camp only
Source: Computing center staff, Outreach program staff

Checklist item: Housing: plan staff and camper space
Brief example: One university uses one floor for staff and other floors for campers
Variant note: On-campus camp only

Checklist item: Meals: decide between dining hall, catering, or packed lunches
Brief example: Dining halls can handle dietary needs; summer dining hours may be limited
Variant note: Half-day workshops may only need snacks or lunch

Checklist item: Meals: collect dietary and allergy information
Brief example: Do this before the event

Checklist item: Transportation: decide who gets students to and from the site
Brief example: Parents drop off and pick up, or the program arranges a bus

Checklist item: Transportation: book buses early if you need them
Brief example: Summer programs compete for charter buses
Variant note: Only if students travel off site

Checklist item: Check the campus rules for payments and cash
Brief example: Credit card processing and cash handling rules

Checklist item: If offering academic credit, work with Admissions and the Registrar
Brief example: Students may need to be admitted first, then register for credit

Checklist item: Set up registration or applications and a way to select students
Brief example: One computing center used a scoring rubric after receiving far more applications than spots

Checklist item: Write a plan B and emergency protocols
Brief example: Backup for equipment, weather, staffing, and schedule changes

Checklist item: Contact your youth protection office early
Brief example: One university requires registering youth events at least 60 days before the start; check your campus's lead time
Variant note: Ask how a short visit is treated

Checklist item: Search with these terms: youth protection, minors on campus, university programs with minors
Brief example: Exact office names may vary by campus. If you cannot find an office, try the risk management office, HEPNet, or NCMEC. These sources have best practices for working with youth

Checklist item: Read your campus minors on campus policy and forms
Brief example: Behavioral forms and training are often available from the office
Source: Outreach coordinator, Computing center staff, Outreach program staff

Checklist item: Check IRB requirements
Brief example: Camps themselves are usually not research; IRB may apply if you collect demographics, quotes, or survey data, or want to publish results
Source: Faculty member, Computing center staff, Outreach coordinator

Checklist item: Ask your IRB whether a student evaluation form counts as research
Get parental permission before the event
Brief example: Permission slips, medical release, health form, and who may pick up students
Source: Computing center staff, High school educator, University compliance staff

Checklist item: Use a code of conduct that students and parents sign
Brief example: Students who break rules can be sent home

Checklist item: Keep contact information and medical needs for each student
Complete compliance training for event staff
Brief example: Mandated reporter, minors on campus, and similar trainings; one university requires training every two years
Source: University compliance staff, Computing center staff, Outreach coordinator

Checklist item: Run background checks for staff with significant access to youth
Brief example: One university's programs pay for checks, and only certain people need them
Variant note: Ask how guest speakers are handled

Checklist item: Plan for CPR and first aid training
Brief example: One university: events of 3 or more days or nights need someone with CPR and first aid training
Source: University compliance staff, Faculty member, Outreach coordinator

Checklist item: Stock first aid supplies
Brief example: One university's rule: 1 first aid kit for every 25 kids

Checklist item: Write an emergency plan
Brief example: The program director creates the plan

Checklist item: Check whether your state requires a license for overnight camps
Brief example: In one state, overnight camps need a license from the state Department of Agriculture and stricter ratios
Variant note: On-campus camp only

Checklist item: Set overnight supervision rules
Brief example: Staff do room checks but do not enter rooms where minors are staying
Variant note: On-campus camp only

Checklist item: Talk to General Counsel, especially for overnight programs
Brief example: Policies can change, so stay in contact

Checklist item: Plan enough time for background checks and training
Brief example: A common mistake is not giving enough time

Checklist item: Ask every student what support they need to succeed
Brief example: Ask 'what kind of help do you need to succeed' rather than 'what accommodations do you need'

Checklist item: Build in flexibility and universal design
Brief example: Universal design makes things more accessible for everyone

Checklist item: Do not label part of the program as 'for people with disabilities'
Brief example: One interviewee said this creates segregation and prevents engagement

Checklist item: Plan accommodations at least 6 to 8 weeks before the start
Brief example: Most accommodations are low tech

Checklist item: Check physical access, assistive technology, and internet access
Brief example: Wheelchair access, sign language interpreter, text-to-voice and voice-to-text apps

Checklist item: Find advocates in the school
Brief example: Counselors, disability services, vocational rehabilitation

Checklist item: Plan group pairings without singling anyone out
Brief example: Hands-on activities may need a helper or second instructor

Checklist item: Plan for different needs when students stay overnight
Brief example: The unstructured time is harder; consider dietary needs and the whole person
Variant note: On-campus camp only

Checklist item: Reduce barriers to participation
Brief example: Transportation, cost, and meeting places near higher-need areas

Checklist item: Make clear in your advertising that everyone is welcome
Brief example: Share through school advocates

Checklist item: Plan pre and post surveys
Brief example: Collect data you will use to improve the program

Checklist item: Collect stories and quotes to report impact
Brief example: Testimonials, thank-you notes, whiteboard videos
Variant note: Check IRB before sharing quotes outside
Source: Faculty member, Outreach coordinator, Computing center staff

Checklist item: Plan how and to whom you will report results
Brief example: Annual report to deans, thank-you letters to sponsors, conference presentations

Checklist item: Use teachers, counselors, and district channels
Brief example: Some districts distribute flyers, and need lead time during the school year

Checklist item: Ask your campus pre-college or marketing office to advertise
Brief example: Programs at two universities were marketed by the campus pre-college program

Checklist item: Choose one person to communicate with parents
Brief example: So families know whom to contact

Checklist item: Create a flyer and plan outreach
Brief example: Flyers, tabling, social media, and local websites

Checklist item: Plan how to handle more applicants than spots
Brief example: Create a rubric before you review applications
